title: Segments, Structure & Anomalies
subtitle: Black Friday is this Friday, the boss can fund four campaigns, and nobody has labeled a single customer. Tonight: no answer column at all. Turn a real gift shop's receipts into customers, find the segments with k-means, choose k like T-shirt sizes, see shapes k-means can't, aim PCA's flashlight at nine columns, and let Isolation Forest play 20 Questions with the receipts

objectives.title: Turn Receipts Into Customers
objectives.description: One groupby squeezes 400,000 receipt lines from a real UK gift shop into 4,312 customers, each described by three numbers: Recency, Frequency, Monetary. Then log and standardize, because unscaled, three whales become their own segment.

objectives.title: Find Segments With k-Means
objectives.description: A party with no name tags: place k hosts, everyone walks to the nearest, hosts move to the middle, repeat. Elbow and silhouette say 3 or 4; the boss can fund four campaigns. Four named segments, one Black Friday action each: 1 customer in 7 brings in 2 pounds in 3.

objectives.title: See Shapes and Many Columns
objectives.description: DBSCAN finds crowds and loners (323 big customers drifting away), the family tree lets you cut at any height, a Gaussian mixture says "maybe". PCA is the flashlight: 9 columns, one picture that keeps 61% of the spread, axes named by their loadings.

objectives.title: Find What Doesn't Belong
objectives.description: Isolation Forest plays 20 Questions: strange receipts are cornered in a few random questions. With no labels it puts bookkeeping entries ("Manual", "Adjustment by Peter") in 49 of its 50 strangest. Strange is not wrong: it's a short list for a human.

agenda.title: Milestone 2 Check-In & Learning Without Answers

bulletPoints: Unsupervised learning finds groups, directions and oddballs; the business supplies the meaning
Tonight you play first: five small games in the Segments Explorer, one before each idea

agenda.title: From Receipts to Customers
agenda.description: Meet a real UK online gift shop: 525,461 receipt lines, Dec 2009 – Dec 2010. Drop guest checkouts (21% of rows) and cancellations, squeeze each customer into Recency, Frequency, Monetary, and meet the whales. Unscaled, k-means makes a segment of three people; log + standardize fixes it.
bulletPoints: Coffee shop owner: was here yesterday, comes every morning, spends a lot
Height in meters vs. weight in grams: put every column in one currency before measuring distance

agenda.title: k-Means: The Party With No Name Tags
agenda.description: Station 1: place four hosts yourself and try to beat the computer. Then the recipe (hosts, nearest, middle, repeat), total walking (inertia) falling every round, and the two traps: a bad start (k-means++, n_init=10) and unscaled columns.
bulletPoints: k-means always finds k groups, even in data that has none

agenda.title: How Many Segments? The Black Friday Plan
agenda.description: Station 2: how many T-shirt sizes? The elbow bends at 3–4, the silhouette peaks at 3 (0.41) and is 0.37 at 4; the boss can fund four campaigns. Name the segments (Champions, Loyal, New & occasional, Hibernating), meet the most typical real customer in each, and give each segment one Black Friday action.
bulletPoints: Champions are 14% of customers and 64% of revenue
The typical Champion restocks about once a month; the typical Hibernating customer bought metal signs on April 1, 2010, and never came back

agenda.title: Other Shapes: Crowds, a Family Tree, and "Maybe"
agenda.description: Station 3: shapes k-means can't see. DBSCAN follows two moons and sets loners aside; on our customers its 323 loners are big spenders drifting away. The dendrogram cuts at any height. A Gaussian mixture says customer 12347 is half Champion, half New.
bulletPoints: DBSCAN's reach (eps) and crowd size (min_samples) replace k
About 1 customer in 7 sits on a border between segments

agenda.title: The Flashlight: PCA
agenda.description: Station 4: turn and tilt 400 customers in 3-D until the shadow keeps the most. Then 9 columns per customer: PC1 keeps 43%, PC1 + PC2 keep 61%. Loadings name the axes: "how big a customer" and "many small visits vs. a few big baskets". UMAP as a subway map, optional.
bulletPoints: Cluster on the scaled features, draw on the PCA picture

agenda.title: 20 Questions: Isolation Forest
agenda.description: Station 5: an ordinary receipt takes about 11 random questions to corner, a strange one about 4. Isolation Forest scores 19,213 receipts with no labels and finds the bookkeeping hiding among the sales, plus £295 kitchen cabinets that are real, just rare. The alert budget (contamination) is a business decision.
bulletPoints: Of the 50 strangest receipts, 49 contain a bookkeeping line; overall only 7% do
Strange is not wrong: a short list for a human

activities.title: From Receipts to a Black Friday Plan
activities.description: Build RFM for every customer of the gift shop, scale it, choose k with the elbow, the silhouette and the boss's budget, name the segments, then let Isolation Forest check the receipts. Each step is in the notebook.

steps.title: Receipts → customers
steps.description: Drop rows with no customer ID and cancellations (invoice starts with 'C'). Group by customer: Recency = days since the last receipt, Frequency = number of receipts, Monetary = total £.

steps.title: One currency
steps.description: log1p on Frequency and Monetary, then StandardScaler on all three. Without it, three whales become a segment of their own.

steps.title: Choose k
steps.description: KMeans(n_init=10) for k = 2…8; plot inertia and silhouette. The data says 3 or 4; four campaigns settles it.

steps.title: Name, act, check
steps.description: Median R, F, M, size and share of revenue per segment. A name and one action each. Then score every receipt with IsolationForest and read the strangest ones.

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

URL = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harslan/isom-835/master/public/data/online_retail_2010.csv.gz'
receipts = pd.read_csv(URL, parse_dates=['InvoiceDate'])
sales = receipts.dropna(subset=['Customer ID'])
sales = sales[~sales['Invoice'].astype(str).str.startswith('C') & (sales['Quantity'] > 0) & (sales['Price'] > 0)].copy()
sales['Amount'] = sales['Quantity'] * sales['Price']
today = pd.Timestamp('2010-12-10')

rfm = sales.groupby('Customer ID').agg(
    Recency=('InvoiceDate', lambda d: (today - d.max()).days),
    Frequency=('Invoice', 'nunique'),
    Monetary=('Amount', 'sum'))
Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.column_stack([rfm['Recency'], np.log1p(rfm['Frequency']), np.log1p(rfm['Monetary'])]))

rfm['segment'] = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=835).fit_predict(Z)
print(rfm.groupby('segment').agg(customers=('Recency', 'size'), days_since=('Recency', 'median'),
      receipts=('Frequency', 'median'), spend=('Monetary', 'median'), revenue=('Monetary', 'sum')).round(0))

activities.discussionNote: Read the money column first: about 1 customer in 7, the Champions, brings in about 2 pounds in 3, while the Hibernating fifth brings in 4 pennies in the pound. Now the four sentences that make it a deliverable: Champions get VIP early access, no discount needed; Loyal get "spend £X, free shipping"; New & occasional get a second-purchase coupon; Hibernating get one cheap email. A segmentation is only as good as the actions that follow it.

takeaways.text: Rows to customers, then one currency, then k-means. Unscaled, three whales made their own segment. k-means always finds k groups: elbow and silhouette say what is reasonable, the business decides.

Other shapes, other tools; PCA is the flashlight. DBSCAN finds crowds and loners, the dendrogram cuts at any height, a mixture says "maybe". Cluster on the features, draw on the PCA picture, name the axes from the loadings.
Isolation Forest plays 20 Questions. With no labels it found the bookkeeping hiding among the sales. Strange is not wrong: the alert budget is a business choice, and a person checks the list.
